S, because it is the larger atom and holds more electrons in total
Neither, because a bond between two nonmetals has no polarity

Polar covalent: the electrons spend more time near one atom
Metallic: the valence electrons are spread over many atoms

items.q: Which statements correctly describe the bonding shown in Box 2? Select all that apply.
options: The valence electrons are delocalized over many cations.
Each electron is held between one particular pair of atoms.
The cations are held together by their attraction to the electrons around them.
Positive and negative ions alternate in fixed positions.
The bonding forms between atoms with a large electronegativity difference.

items.q: Which statement describes a covalent bond?
options: A pair of electrons held by one atom and not attracted by the other
The attraction between a cation and an anion after an electron moves
Cations held together by electrons that move through the whole sample
A pair of electrons shared by two atoms and attracted by both nuclei

options: NF₃
CaF₂
CS₂
SiCl₄

items.q: When sodium reacts with chlorine, an electron moves from Na to Cl. Which explanation is best?
options: Na wants a full outer shell, so it chooses to give its single valence electron away to the nearest atom it meets
Na's valence electron is far from its nucleus and shielded, so it is held weakly; Cl's nucleus attracts one strongly
Cl already has more electrons than Na, so Cl has more electrons of its own with which to attract the extra one
Na is the larger atom, so it has more room to lose an electron than a small Cl atom has to lose one of its own

Number of electrons shared between H and the halogen

items.q: Which description of the dipole arrow for an H–F bond is correct?
options: The arrow points from F to H, because H gives up electron density
The arrow points from F to H, with the crossed tail at the F end
No arrow is drawn, because H and F are both nonmetals
The arrow points from H to F, with the crossed tail at the H end

items.q: Magnesium oxide and copper are both solids. A student says both are held together by ionic bonds because both contain positive ions. Which response is correct?
options: Copper is metallic: delocalized electrons hold its cations
The student is right: any solid that contains positive ions is ionic
Magnesium oxide is metallic, since magnesium is itself a metal
Both are covalent, since the atoms in each of them share electrons

items.q: What is the bond length of the molecule shown by Curve 2?
options: About 436 pm
About 74 pm
About 30 pm
About 400 pm

items.q: About how much energy is needed to separate one mole of the Curve 1 molecules into free atoms?
options: About 0 kJ
About 200 kJ
About 480 kJ
About 240 kJ

items.q: On Curve 2, why does the potential energy rise steeply at distances shorter than 74 pm?
options: The nuclei, and the electron clouds, repel more strongly as they are pushed together
The bond breaks at short distances, so the atoms fly apart and the energy goes up
The attraction between each nucleus and the shared electrons grows weaker as they approach
The atoms lose their valence electrons when they get too close to each other

items.q: Curve 1 is Cl₂ and Curve 2 is H₂. Which explanation for the longer bond in Cl₂ is best?
options: Cl₂ has a greater mass, and a heavier molecule has a longer bond
Cl atoms have more protons, so their two nuclei attract each other and pull the bonded atoms apart
Cl's valence electrons are in the third shell, far from the nucleus, so the nuclei settle farther apart
The bond in Cl₂ is weaker, and a weaker bond has to be a longer bond

items.q: The bond energy of H₂ is 436 kJ/mol. How much energy is needed to break the bonds in 0.250 mol of H₂? Include the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by 0.250 instead of multiplying. Energy per mole times moles gives energy.

items.q: Which statement describes the trend for carbon-carbon bonds?
options: From single to triple, the bond gets shorter and weaker
From single to triple, the bond gets longer and stronger
From single to triple, the bond gets shorter and stronger
The length changes, but the bond energy stays about the same

items.q: Why is a C=O double bond shorter than a C–O single bond?
options: Four shared electrons attract both nuclei more strongly than two, pulling them closer
The oxygen atom shrinks when it forms a double bond, so the two nuclei can come closer
A double bond is two separate single bonds, each half the length of a single bond
The double bond has less energy, so it takes up less room between the two atoms

items.q: How much more energy, in kJ, is needed to break 1.00 mol of N≡N bonds than 1.00 mol of N–N bonds?

mistakes.why: Value: you added the two bond energies. The question asks for the difference: subtract.

items.q: The potential energy curves for C–C and C≡C are drawn on the same axes. How does the C≡C curve compare?
options: Its minimum is at the same place, but the curve is narrower
Its minimum is deeper and farther to the right
Its minimum is shallower and farther to the left
Its minimum is deeper and farther to the left

items.q: A nitrogen-nitrogen bond is changed from a double bond (N=N) to a triple bond (N≡N). Predict the change in each quantity.

variables.name: Energy needed to break 1 mol of the bonds
Number of protons in each nitrogen nucleus

items.q: Which is an intramolecular force?
options: An attraction between one water molecule and a different water molecule
The covalent bond holding O and H together inside one water molecule
The pull of Earth's gravity on a sample of water in a glass
The push that a liquid exerts on the walls of its container

items.q: Two hydrogen atoms far apart move toward each other and form H₂. Which statement about energy is correct?
options: Energy is absorbed, because forming a bond takes energy
Energy is released, because the bonded atoms have lower potential energy
No energy changes, because the same atoms are present before and after
Energy is released, because the bond breaks as the atoms get close

items.q: Ion pairs are compared at their usual center-to-center distances: Na⁺ and F⁻ (231 pm), and Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ (210 pm). Which pair attracts more strongly, and why?
options: The attractions are equal, because each pair has one cation and one anion
Na⁺ and F⁻: F is the most electronegative element, so F⁻ attracts most strongly
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻: the ions are heavier, so they attract each other more
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻: both charges are larger and the ions are closer together

items.q: The centers of Na⁺ and F⁻ are 231 pm apart in sodium fluoride, and those of Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are 210 pm apart in magnesium oxide. Using Coulomb's law, F ∝ q₁q₂/r², how many times stronger is the Mg²⁺–O²⁻ attraction than the Na⁺–F⁻ attraction?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by r instead of r². Coulomb's force falls with the square of the distance.
Value: you put the distance ratio upside down. The closer pair (210 pm) attracts more, so the ratio (231/210)² is greater than 1.
Value: you compared the charges only. The Mg²⁺–O²⁻ ions are also closer together, which makes the force even larger.

items.q: The bond energy of HCl is 431 kJ/mol. How much energy is needed to break the bond in one HCl molecule? Give the answer in joules, in scientific notation, with the unit.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by Avogadro's number. One molecule is a tiny fraction of a mole, so divide by 6.022 × 10²³.

items.q: Which feature of a potential energy curve for two bonded atoms gives the bond energy? Select all that apply.
options: The depth of the minimum below zero
The distance at which the minimum occurs
The height of the curve at the shortest distance shown
The distance at which the curve first reaches zero

items.q: Which statement best explains why NaF melts at a higher temperature than NaCl?
options: F is more electronegative than Cl, so it holds the shared electrons more tightly
F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻, so the ions are closer and attract more strongly
NaF has a smaller molar mass, and lighter compounds have higher melting temperatures
F⁻ has a larger charge than Cl⁻, so its attraction to each Na⁺ ion is stronger

items.q: MgO and NaF have ions about the same distance apart, yet MgO melts about 1900 °C higher. Which explanation is best?
options: MgO has more ions per formula unit than NaF, so there are more bonds to break
Mg²⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, so the MgO ions are much closer together than the NaF ions
O is less electronegative than F, so MgO is a more ionic compound overall than NaF
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have twice the charges of Na⁺ and F⁻, so they attract far more strongly

items.q: Using charges and distances only, put these compounds in order of lattice energy, from smallest to largest.
options: KCl
NaCl
CaO
MgO

items.q: A student says KCl melts lower than NaCl "because K⁺ is bigger." Which version of this claim would earn full credit on a free-response answer?
options: Same charges (1+, 1−), but K⁺ is larger than Na⁺, so K⁺ and Cl⁻ are farther apart and attract less
K is a bigger atom than Na, so KCl is a bigger compound and is held together less tightly
K⁺ is bigger than Na⁺, so it has more electrons, which repel the Cl⁻ ions and weaken the bonds
K is lower in group 1 than Na, so KCl is made of molecules held by weaker forces than NaCl

items.q: The substance in Box 2 conducts electricity but the substance in Box 1 does not. Which explanation is correct?
options: Box 2 has more ions than Box 1, so it can carry a much larger current
In Box 2 the electrons are free to move, as in a metal, but in Box 1 they are not
In Box 2 the ions can move and carry charge; in Box 1 they are held in place
Box 1 is made of neutral atoms, while Box 2 is made of charged ions

items.q: What is wrong with Box 3 as a model of solid sodium chloride?
options: It shows separate pairs, but each ion attracts several opposite-charge neighbors
It shows the wrong ratio of ions: solid sodium chloride has two Cl⁻ ions per Na⁺ ion
The ions should be drawn the same size, because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ have the same number of electrons
Nothing is wrong: an ionic compound is made of molecules, each one cation and one anion

items.q: In Box 1, how many Cl⁻ ions are nearest neighbors of the Na⁺ ion in the second row, second column?
A crystal of salt shatters when struck with a hammer. Which explanation is best?
options: Salt is held together by weak forces that are easily overcome by a sharp force
The blow breaks the covalent bonds between the sodium and chlorine atoms
The blow knocks electrons off the ions, so the crystal is no longer held together
The blow shifts a layer of ions so that like charges line up and repel

items.q: Calcium bromide, CaBr₂, is an ionic compound. Which samples conduct electricity? Select all that apply.
options: Solid CaBr₂ at room temperature
Molten (melted) CaBr₂
CaBr₂ dissolved in water
A dry crystal of CaBr₂ after it is ground to powder

items.q: Which description fits an ionic solid?
options: Separate molecules, each one made of a single cation stuck to one anion
A repeating 3-D array of cations and anions, each next to opposite charges
Metal cations in a sea of electrons that move through the whole solid
Atoms joined by shared pairs of electrons into a single large molecule

items.q: Which compound is expected to have the largest lattice energy?
options: MgCl₂
Al₂O₃
NaBr
KI

items.q: Compare lithium fluoride (LiF) with cesium fluoride (CsF). Going from LiF to CsF, predict the change in each quantity.

items.q: Why does an ionic solid such as NaCl have a high melting temperature?
options: Ionic solids are dense, and a denser solid needs more heat to melt
Each Na–Cl molecule is held together by a very strong covalent bond
The electrons moving through the solid hold the ions firmly in place
Each ion is held by many oppositely charged neighbors at once

items.q: Use Coulomb's law (F ∝ q₁q₂/r²) to find how many times stronger the attraction between neighboring ions is in CaO (centers 240 pm apart) than in KCl (centers 315 pm apart).

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by r instead of r². The force falls with the square of the distance.
Value: you compared the charges only. The CaO ions are also closer, which makes the attraction stronger still.
Value: the distance ratio is upside down. The closer pair (CaO) attracts more, so use (315/240)².

items.q: Which property is expected for solid potassium iodide, KI?
options: It is hard and brittle and does not conduct as a solid
It bends without breaking and conducts electricity as a solid
It is soft and it melts at a temperature below 25 °C
It conducts electricity as a solid but not when melted

Box X

Potassium, K
Boron, B
Chromium, Cr

items.q: The material in Box X is harder and less malleable than the material in Box W. Which explanation is best?
options: Carbon atoms in the gaps block the iron layers from sliding past each other
The carbon atoms take electrons from the sea, so fewer electrons hold iron together
The carbon atoms make the iron atoms larger, so the iron atoms pack more tightly
Carbon is a nonmetal, so its atoms form ionic bonds with the iron atoms

items.q: Which statements are true of all three samples in boxes W, X and Y? Select all that apply.
options: They conduct electricity because they contain delocalized electrons.
Their atoms are held together by metallic bonding.
They are made of a single element.
They contain atoms of two different sizes in the gaps between atoms.

items.q: In Box Y, what percent of the atoms are atoms of the second metal?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by the number of iron atoms (15). Divide by the total number of atoms (20).

items.q: Which kind of alloy are brass and bronze, based on the atomic radii?
options: Interstitial: the added atoms are larger than Cu atoms
Interstitial: the added atoms fit into the gaps between Cu atoms
Substitutional: the added atoms are close in size to Cu
Neither: an alloy needs a nonmetal to be added

items.q: Which claim about the data is best supported, with the right reasoning?
options: Brass is harder because Zn atoms are closer in size to Cu, so they bond more strongly
Bronze is harder because it contains more of the added metal than brass does
Bronze is harder because Sn differs more in size from Cu and disrupts the layers more
The three are about equally hard, since each wire still bends without breaking

items.q: Why can all three wires bend without breaking, unlike a crystal of an ionic solid?
options: As layers slide, the electron sea still surrounds each cation, so the bonding holds
The metals contain covalent bonds, which can bend without breaking
Metal atoms carry no charge, so they do not repel each other when the layers move
The wires are thin, and any thin solid bends rather than breaks

items.q: All three wires conduct electricity well. Which feature of their structure explains this?
options: Pairs of electrons shared between two atoms
Cations and anions that are free to move about
Small atoms sitting in the gaps of the lattice
Delocalized electrons that can move through the solid

items.q: Gold can be hammered into a sheet thin enough to see light through. Which explanation is best?
options: Gold is soft because its metallic bonds are much weaker than any other bonds
Its layers of atoms slide past each other while the electron sea holds them together
Gold atoms are very large, so there is a lot of empty space for them to move into
Each gold atom is bonded to just one neighbor, so the atoms are free to move about

items.q: Steel for cutting tools is made by adding a small amount of carbon to iron. How does adding carbon change the iron?
options: It becomes softer and more malleable
It becomes harder and less malleable
It stops conducting electricity
It becomes brittle like an ionic solid, shattering when struck

items.q: A metallurgist adds a small amount of nitrogen (radius 71 pm) to pure iron (126 pm). Predict how each property changes.

variables.name: Number of iron atoms in each layer of the lattice

items.q: What is an alloy?
options: A metal whose atoms have been turned into anions by gaining electrons
A compound of a metal and a nonmetal with a fixed formula
A pure metal that has been melted down and then cooled again into a new shape
A mixture of a metal with other elements that keeps metallic properties

items.q: Which properties can both pure metals and their alloys be expected to have? Select all that apply.
options: Good electrical conductivity
Good thermal conductivity
A single fixed formula
Brittleness

items.q: Sterling silver is 92.5% silver (atomic radius 144 pm) and 7.5% copper (128 pm). Which classification and reasoning is best?
options: Substitutional: Cu atoms are close enough in size to Ag atoms to take their places
Interstitial: Cu atoms are smaller than Ag atoms, so they go into the gaps between them
Interstitial: there is much less copper than silver, so the copper fills the gaps
Substitutional: Cu and Ag are in the same group, so their alloys are substitutional

Diagram 3
Diagram 2

items.q: In Diagram 4, how many electrons surround the boron atom, and what does this show?

Eight, because each atom in a molecule has an octet
Six, so the diagram has to be wrong
Six, an incomplete octet, which boron can have

items.q: In Diagram 2 (H₂CO), how many lone pairs are on the whole molecule?
How does the C atom in Diagram 1 (HCN) reach an octet?

It has two lone pairs plus two single bonds to H and N

items.q: How many valence electrons must the Lewis diagram of the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, show?

mistakes.why: Value: you left out the charge. A 2− charge means two extra electrons: add 2 to the atoms' 30.
Value: you subtracted 2 for the charge. A 2− ion has gained two electrons: add 2.

items.q: How many valence electrons must the Lewis diagram of the borohydride ion, BH₄⁻, show?

mistakes.why: Value: you subtracted an electron for the 1− charge. A negative ion has gained an electron: add 1.

items.q: Which species in the table cannot have every atom with an octet in its Lewis diagram?
options: BH₄⁻
PCl₃
NO
SO₄²⁻

items.q: In SF₆, sulfur forms six bonds. Which statement is correct?
options: SF₆ is not a real compound, as S would break the octet rule
S has 8 electrons, because each bond counts as one electron for S
S has 12 electrons, an expanded octet, possible in period 3
S has 12 electrons, and each F has an expanded octet too

items.q: In a Lewis diagram, what does a lone pair represent?
options: Two valence electrons on one atom, not shared
Two electrons shared between two atoms in a bond
Two core electrons held close to the nucleus
A single unpaired electron on one atom

items.q: Put the steps for drawing a Lewis diagram in order.
options: Count the valence electrons, adjusting for any charge
Place the central atom and connect each outer atom with a single bond
Complete the octets of the outer atoms with lone pairs
Put any electrons left over on the central atom
If the central atom lacks an octet, turn outer lone pairs into double or triple bonds

items.q: What is the correct Lewis diagram for carbon dioxide, CO₂?
options: O≡C–O, with one lone pair on the triple-bonded O and two on the other
O–C–O, with three lone pairs on each O and no lone pair on C
O–C–O, with three lone pairs on each O and two on C
O=C=O, with two lone pairs on each O

items.q: A student drew the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, as N bonded to four H atoms with one lone pair on N. What is wrong?
options: It has too few electrons; N needs two lone pairs
It shows 10 electrons; NH₄⁺ has 8, so no lone pair
Nothing is wrong; N keeps its one lone pair
H atoms need lone pairs to complete their octets

items.q: Which of these molecules has a central atom with an expanded octet in its Lewis diagram? Select all that apply.
options: PCl₅
CCl₄
NF₃
BCl₃

items.q: Draw the Lewis diagram of nitrogen trichloride, NCl₃. How many lone pairs does the whole molecule have?

mistakes.why: Value: you counted the chlorine lone pairs only. N also keeps one lone pair: 26 electrons − 6 in bonds = 20 = 10 pairs.

items.q: Which is the correct skeleton (arrangement of atoms) for the hypochlorous acid molecule, HOCl?
options: H–Cl–O, with Cl as the central atom
H–O–Cl, with O as the central atom
O–H–Cl, with H as the central atom
Cl–O and H unbonded beside them

items.q: Which is the correct Lewis diagram for the cyanide ion, CN⁻?
options: [C–N]⁻ with three lone pairs on each atom
[C≡N]⁻ with no lone pairs on either atom
[C=N]⁻ with two lone pairs on each atom
[C≡N]⁻ with one lone pair on each atom

items.q: What is the formal charge on the N atom in Structure I? Give a sign with your answer (for example −1).

mistakes.why: Sign: you subtracted the other way. Formal charge = valence electrons − lone-pair electrons − half the bonding electrons = 5 − 4 − 2.

items.q: What is the formal charge on the O atom in Structure III? Give a sign with your answer.

mistakes.why: Sign: O has fewer electrons assigned to it (2 + 3 = 5) than its 6 valence electrons, so its formal charge is positive.

items.q: Which structure best represents the cyanate ion, and why?
options: Structure I: it has two double bonds, and a symmetrical structure is the most stable
Structure II: small formal charges, with the −1 on O, the most electronegative atom
Structure III: it has a triple bond, which is the strongest kind of bond
Structure I: N carries the negative charge, and N is the larger of the two outer atoms

items.q: Which statements are true of all three structures? Select all that apply.
options: The formal charges add up to −1.
Each structure uses exactly 16 valence electrons.
Each atom has a formal charge of zero.
The C atom has a lone pair.

items.q: Structures I and II differ only in where electrons are placed. Which statement about the real cyanate ion is best?
options: Half of the ions in a sample are Structure I and half are Structure II at any moment
It switches back and forth between Structure I and Structure II many times each second
It is exactly Structure II; Structures I and III are mistakes that do not describe the ion
It is one hybrid, closest to Structure II, with electrons delocalized over O, C and N

items.q: One Lewis diagram of ozone shows one O–O single bond and one O=O double bond. Which statement about the measured data is best?
options: Both are 128 pm, between single (148) and double (121): ozone is a resonance hybrid
One bond should measure 148 pm and the other 121 pm, so the data are in error
